title: Towards an autonomous optomechanical Maxwell Demon engine
authors: Sander Stammbach, Giulio Gasbarri, Stefan Nimmrichter
abstract: We present a fully autonomous model of a mechanical Maxwell demon engine that converts heat absorbed by a qubit into population inversion in an attached quantum battery. A damped mechanical oscillator acts as a pointer that incorporates the essential demon function of information acquisition about the qubit state and subsequent feedback into the system dynamics, replacing external measurements and control operations. This is achieved by means of a Holstein-type Hamiltonian, which makes the pointer's equilibrium position depend on the qubit state and thereby induces a state-dependent resonance shift. The mechanism enables a selective energy transfer to an attached spin system that acts as the quantum battery. We derive both local and global Lindblad master equations for the coupled system and identify the parameter regimes in which the engine operates efficiently. The figure of merit is the resulting steady-state population inversion of the battery, quantified in terms of ergotropy. Based on these results, we discuss the necessary conditions for practical implementations of the demon engine on realistic experimental platforms.
summary: This paper models a quantum engine based on a mechanical Maxwell Demon, where a qubit interacts with a mechanical oscillator pointer to extract energy from a thermal bath. The pointer acts autonomously by conditioning the qubit's energy transfer to a quantum battery, allowing the system to perform work continuously. The analysis uses advanced master equation techniques to confirm the operational feasibility and quantify the extracted energy.
main_problem: The paper develops a fully autonomous model of a mechanical Maxwell demon engine designed to convert heat absorbed by a qubit into useful work stored in an attached quantum battery.
main_result: The system successfully operates as a continuous thermal machine, demonstrating energy extraction quantified by the battery's steady-state ergotropy, all driven by the internal information processing of the mechanical pointer.
method: The dynamics are analyzed using Lindblad master equations (local, global, and TCL2 forms) to model the coupled system, comparing theoretical predictions against established thermodynamic principles.
model_or_system: The model consists of three coupled components: a qubit (working medium), a damped mechanical oscillator (the information-acquiring pointer), and a quantum battery (spin system). The coupling is governed by a Holstein-type Hamiltonian, enabling state-dependent resonance shifts.
key_observables: Steady-state population inversion of the battery (quantified by ergotropy), energy currents ($	ext{J}_h, 	ext{J}_c$), and entropy production ($\Sigma$).

main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the pointer relaxation is fast compared to qubit dynamics, and it compares results derived from various master equation approximations (Local vs. Global BMS vs. TCL2).
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the coupled system (qubit, oscillator, battery) and show time evolution plots comparing population dynamics predicted by different master equation formalisms.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical model and the autonomous mechanism using the Holstein Hamiltonian. It then derives the necessary master equations, analyzes the resonance condition, and finally discusses the comparison between different theoretical descriptions (Lindblad vs. TCL2) and potential experimental platforms.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium thermodynamics and information theory by building a quantum mechanical realization of a classical concept (Maxwell's Demon), which is highly relevant to open quantum systems and energy transduction.
